Author: <git.Actor "jaisurya93945 <jaisurya3450@gmail.com>">
Date: 2026-09-12 05:43:26+00:00
Message: 'feat: measure contract drafting against MCP schemas we did not write

Every previous measurement of the deriver used a corpus we authored, and
BENCHMARKS.md has said so since the corpus existed. This replaces the excuse
with data: `tools/list` captured over stdio from seven published MCP servers,
52 tools and 94 parameters, checked in so the measurement reproduces offline.

The headline is not a score. It is that MCP carries an effect signal this
project had said could not exist, and that believing it naively would be a
total bypass:

  51 of 52 tools carry `annotations`
  32 of 52 claim `readOnlyHint: true`

A monitor that believed that hint would have disabled its own confidentiality
rules on 62% of this corpus on day one. So annotations are read under a
direction test rather than a trust decision -- an annotation may ADD an effect
and may never remove one. `destructiveHint` and `openWorldHint` are believed,
because a hostile server lying that way only denies its own tools;
`readOnlyHint` is ignored outright. The rule generalises past MCP: it is the
condition under which any attacker-controllable metadata is safe to read.
Believing only the restrictive half completed 8 of 52 drafts that would
otherwise have carried no effects at all.

Four defects the real schemas found, none of which a corpus we wrote would
have:

  * `"type": ["string", "null"]` crashed the deriver. JSON Schema's `type` is
    a string *or a list*. Unions are now downgraded only when every member is
    a type that cannot hold an identifier.
  * camelCase was invisible: hints split on `_` only, so `sortBy` stayed
    AUTHORITY while `sort_by` was advisory, and `fileId` missed the identifier
    suffix `file_id` matched. Every JavaScript server names things this way.
  * the linter reported the `unclassified` pseudo-kind as an unregistered
    kind, at ERROR severity, on 23 of 94 parameters -- a quarter of an
    operator's first run, all wrong, on the checks that exist to be trusted.
  * `branchId` drafted the collection `**.branchs`, which matches nothing and
    makes reference binding silently never fire for that parameter.

And one uncomfortable result, recorded rather than smoothed over: reference
binding's collection draft fires on 2 of 60 authority parameters here.
Published servers name things `path`, `repo_path` and `branch_name`, not
`<noun>_id`. It was designed against AgentDojo's keyed dictionaries, and the
servers people actually deploy are not shaped that way. ADR-0011 is qualified
accordingly.

CI now replays the corpus and fails on any parameter reported as an
unregistered kind, which is the defect above turned into a regression test.
'

Commit: '1957c33e8f7ca19594dd46b3d8b466e7389e89e8'
Author: <git.Actor "jaisurya93945 <jaisurya3450@gmail.com>">
Date: 2026-09-12 05:32:04+00:00
Message: 'feat: bind entity ids to the principal's own reference, and sweep the knobs

The previous milestone named entity selection as the binding constraint and
gave three options: narrow the claim, attack it directly, or stop. This takes
the second. An id is admissible when the principal's own words *name* the
record it identifies -- its title, its filename, its location -- and not when
only an injection did.

Granted per field path as a pseudo-kind (`referenced`), exactly like any other
operand kind, so it is opt-in and costs nothing where it is not declared.

What it is worth, measured rather than assumed:

  workspace suite (where entity selection lives)   70.0% -> 77.5% utility
                                                   100%  -> 100%  security
  all four suites, best configuration >= 90% sec   66.0% -> 68.0% utility

Two tasks out of ninety-seven. It does not clear this project's own 90%/70%
bar; the closest configuration that exists is 91.6%/68.0%.

Three defects in the mechanism were found by measuring it and none by review:

  * whole-field matching fired on *nothing* -- real instructions say "my Dental
    check-up" about a record titled `Dentist Appointment`, so the unit of
    comparison had to become a fragment;
  * ids were bound without their collection, so naming calendar event 13
    authorised deleting file 13 -- the mechanism reproducing the attack it
    exists to refuse. Parameters now declare which directory their id
    addresses, and it fires for none that do not;
  * the new labelling pinned its own quotation floor while the sweep varied
    everyone else's, making its column invariant by construction. That would
    have been published as a finding.

Two more surfaced alongside: reference binding was silently inflating the
utility of labellings that granted nothing through it, and advisory parameter
hints matched names exactly, so `new_start_time` was authority-bearing while
`start_time` was advisory.

Reporting one number per labelling was also wrong. Two policy thresholds move
the result and interact, so BENCHMARKS.md now reports a 6x5 sweep and the
Pareto frontier over all thirty configurations, including the rows where this
design loses. `min_reference_word` moved neither axis at any setting and is
recorded as unpriced rather than as safe.

Also: the proxy could not express path-scoped grants at all, so the
configuration the documentation recommends was unreachable from the shipped
product. `source.authoritative_paths`, `min_quotation_length` and
`min_reference_word` are now config, and the linter reports a `referenced`
grant no parameter can consume -- inert, and therefore denying everything that
path would otherwise have allowed.
'

Commit: 'b9595ce3b75e2353ba35a3fbbf4993e7a4b98955'
Author: <git.Actor "jaisurya93945 <jaisurya3450@gmail.com>">
Date: 2026-09-10 16:59:04+00:00
Message: 'feat: observe dict keys, and measure the security-utility exchange rate

Two changes and one conclusion.

Dict keys were never observed. A tool result shaped as
{"events": {"5": {...}}} carries the entity id in the key, so a walk
that visits only leaves never sees it and every follow-up call on that
entity was attributable to nothing. Keys are now indexed with their
collection path -- indexed rather than sealed, because rewriting a key
would change the structure the agent has to navigate, and attribution
is what refuses an attacker-chosen value anyway. This was the single
largest remaining source of false denials.

The evaluation gains a fourth configuration measuring the documented
treatment of computed magnitudes: amount as content, bounded by a
budget. Banking went from 31.2% to 87.5% utility at 95.8% security.

The conclusion is the point, and it is not a number:

  authority granted        security   utility
  nothing                    95.4%     34.0%
  every kind, everywhere     55.8%     46.4%
  per field path             85.7%     68.0%
  + budgets for magnitudes   85.1%     76.3%

No configuration reaches 90% security and 70% utility together. The
falsification criterion this project set for itself asked for exactly
that, and it was missed on the security side. REVIEW.md says so in its
own title, reports the 95.4% row first in every table, and takes the
option that narrows the claim rather than the one that reinterprets the
number.

Determinism was not the binding constraint. Every bug fixed in this pass
bought utility at zero security cost; security fell only where a human
widened a grant. The constraint is that a large fraction of real agent
work is selecting an existing entity -- reschedule that event, share
that file -- and when the directory is untrusted, provenance must either
refuse the selection or trust the directory, which admits an injection
naming a legitimate entry. That is intent, not origin, so oracle
provenance would not resolve it either.

The claim is therefore narrowed rather than restated, in the README, the
threat model and the limitations: IDENSEC contains attacks that
introduce a new destination, and is structurally blind to attacks that
select among legitimate ones. The cost of that blindness is measured.

Recorded as a hypothesis rather than a criticism: PACT's reported oracle
row of 100/100 is hard to reconcile with entity-selection workflows,
which suggests its diagnostic suites may not contain that pattern. We
cannot check -- the paper is not reachable from this environment.
'

Commit: '13e2cf5d3fccc2a6bb4adaa21759a276bae7cecb'
Author: <git.Actor "jaisurya93945 <jaisurya3450@gmail.com>">
Date: 2026-09-10 11:42:13+00:00
Message: 'fix: collect every matching origin, and normalise numeric spellings

Two defects found by working through AgentDojo's remaining refusals.

Attribution took only the *first* origin from which a value was
derivable. Authority is decided existentially -- a value is admissible
if any contributing source is authorised for it -- so stopping at the
first match hands the checker an unauthorised origin while an authorised
one exists further down. This denied legitimate calls whose entity id
also happened to appear inside an earlier free-text field. All matching
origins are now collected.

Numbers reach tools in more spellings than they appear in prose: a tool
takes 4.0 where the principal wrote 4, or 1200 where they wrote 1,200.
Derivation now generates exact re-spellings of the same number -- no
rounding, no unit conversion, nothing semantic -- and a regression test
confirms the substring-carving bypass stays closed.

Also downgrades two classes of parameter the deriver was over-claiming:
content names such as location and venue, which decide nothing an
attacker benefits from, and filter names such as query and pattern, but
only on read-only tools -- on anything that writes or egresses a "query"
may be a command, so the restrictive reading is kept and the linter's
no-authority-parameter check is the backstop.

Utility 51.5% -> 56.7% at unchanged 92.0% security. Contract derivation
still shows 100% authority recall and zero dangerous misses.

The banking suite's remaining refusals turned out not to be fixable, and
that is the more useful finding: its amounts are *computed*, not quoted.
"Spotify raised prices 10% this month, send them the difference" yields
5.0, which appears nowhere in the instruction. Arithmetic is a semantic
derivation and no provenance system can follow it, so treating an amount
as authority-bearing denies the legitimate case exactly as often as the
attacker's -- accidental security rather than designed security.

The division of labour that does work is now documented and tested:
provenance handles identifiers, budgets handle magnitudes. Let the
amount be payload and bound it with a Budget; the destination is still
attributed, so an attacker-chosen recipient is refused regardless, and
no amount can exceed what the principal allowed.
'

Commit: 'e448c4559d6aa7fe435559cea81de332e7f3f65a'
Author: <git.Actor "jaisurya93945 <jaisurya3450@gmail.com>">
Date: 2026-09-10 11:33:56+00:00
Message: "feat: measure security and utility against AgentDojo, model-free

The utility cost of argument-level enforcement was this project's
largest unknown and was recorded as blocked on model API access. It was
not blocked: AgentDojo publishes both halves as data. Each injection
task carries the tool call the attacker wants; each user task carries
the calls a correct agent makes. Replaying both measures security and
utility with no model anywhere.

Security is asked in a harsher form than AgentDojo's own metric --
AgentDojo measures how often a model is hijacked, we assume it always
is. Utility is a lower bound: ground-truth calls are not model
behaviour.

Result, best labelling, 97 user tasks and 609 in-scope security cases:
92.0% security, 51.5% utility.

Source labelling turned out to be the dominant variable, and per-source
grants the wrong shape. Authoritative-for-nothing gave 95.4%/28.9%.
Authoritative-for-everything gave 68.6%/39.2% -- worse on both axes.
The cause is structural: legitimate addresses live in sender,
recipients and participants while every injection lives in description,
content and reviews, and both arrive from one source. Since provenance
was already recorded per field, authority is now scopable the same way
via Source.authoritative_paths, with segment globs. The travel suite
went from 0% to 100% utility on that change alone. That is a capability
the measurement produced, not a tuning.

Four real defects fell out of contact with somebody else's tools:
recipient constrained to email, which failed every IBAN transfer; url
constrained to url, which failed every scheme-less fetch; temporal
parameters treated as authority-bearing, the single largest source of
false denials; and *_id constrained to the uuid kind. UNCLASSIFIED is
introduced so that values with no surface grammar -- a channel name, a
hotel name -- can be granted rather than being permanently unauthorised.

Every one of the 49 escapes is explained, and all fall into limitations
documented before this measurement existed: 20 where the attacker
selects a legitimate directory entry, 20 where the target call has no
authority-bearing argument, 8 low-entropy token collisions, plus 20
speech-only injections excluded because an action monitor cannot address
speech. The boundary that yields is the most useful output here:
IDENSEC contains attacks that introduce a new destination; it does not
contain attacks that merely select among legitimate ones.

The uncomfortable part is recorded as such rather than as a caveat.
51.5% is nearer PACT's deployed row than its oracle row, and REVIEW.md
set that as the falsification condition before the number existed. The
thesis is not yet disproven -- utility moved 22.7% to 51.5% in one
sitting on obvious fixes and has not converged -- but it is now the only
roadmap item that matters, and leaving it in a table while building
features is the failure mode. LIMITATIONS, RESEARCH, THREAT_MODEL,
REVIEW, ROADMAP and the README all say so.

Effect classes and scoped grants were hand-authored per API by people
who do not own those APIs. That is precisely the policy-sprawl objection
this project claims to answer, and one afternoon for four APIs does not
answer it. benchmarks/agentdojo/README.md names every artefact we
authored, and the pre-tuning number is reported beside the post-tuning
one.
"

Commit: '9e31e7227b67b6c2bb6d187f33467af6567d9ab9'
Author: <git.Actor "jaisurya93945 <jaisurya3450@gmail.com>">
Date: datetime.datetime(2026, 9, 10, 2, 58, 53, tzinfo=<git.objects.util.tzoffset object at 0x7f8cf621f510>)
Message: 'test: fuzz the core invariants with seeded property tests\n\nThe milestone review concluded that every bug found so far lived in code\nthat had been written carefully and tested, and that tests written by\nthe author of a mechanism test the mechanism the author had in mind.\nThis attacks the paths nobody thought to write a test for.\n\nFive invariants, each a real defect if violated: sealing leaves no\nrecognised operand in the text handed to the model; the monitor returns\na verdict rather than raising on arbitrary argument shapes, because a\nmonitor that crashes fails open in any harness that catches exceptions\nand carries on; decisions replay identically including the audit chain\nhead; an authority value from a non-authoritative source is never\nadmitted; and handles resolve to exactly what was sealed.\n\nTwo mirror properties are asserted alongside, because a monitor that\nrefused everything would satisfy the security invariants and be\nworthless: prose carrying no identifiers passes through byte-for-byte,\nand a source that *is* authoritative still works.\n\nSeeded random rather than a property-testing dependency. The library has\nno runtime dependencies and its suite should not need one either, and a\nfixed seed makes a failure reproducible from the test name alone.\n\n204 cases in the suite. A separate campaign over 2000 seeds and 25125\noperations found no violations, which is evidence rather than proof --\nthe generators only produce inputs we thought to generate.\n'

--- None
+++ tests/test_fuzz.py
@@ -0,0 +1,328 @@
+"""Property-based fuzzing of the core invariants.
+
+The milestone review concluded that every bug found so far lived in code that
+had been written carefully and tested, and that tests written by the author of a
+mechanism test the mechanism the author had in mind. This file exists to attack
+the paths nobody thought to write a test for.
+
+Seeded ``random`` rather than a property-testing dependency: the library has no
+runtime dependencies and its test suite should not need one either, and a fixed
+seed makes a failure reproducible from the test name alone. Seeds are listed
+explicitly so a failing case can be re-run in isolation.
+
+Five invariants, each of which would be a real defect if violated:
+
+1. **Sealing is complete.** After observing untrusted content, no operand the
+   extractor recognised survives in the text handed to the model.
+2. **The monitor never raises.** Arbitrary argument shapes produce a verdict,
+   not a traceback -- a monitor that crashes on malformed input fails *open* in
+   any harness that catches exceptions and continues.
+3. **Decisions are deterministic.** The same script always produces the same
+   verdicts and the same audit chain head.
+4. **Untrusted authority is never admitted.** The central security property,
+   asserted against randomly generated attacker content rather than
+   hand-chosen cases.
+5. **Handles round-trip.** Resolving a sealed value returns exactly what was
+   sealed.
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import itertools
+import random
+import string
+
+import pytest
+
+from idensec import (
+    ContractRegistry,
+    Effect,
+    ParameterContract,
+    Policy,
+    Role,
+    Session,
+    Source,
+    ToolContract,
+    Trust,
+    Verdict,
+)
+from idensec.kinds import extract
+from idensec.ledger import SEAL_PATTERN
+
+SEEDS = list(range(24))
+
+TOOLS = [
+    ToolContract(
+        tool="send_email",
+        parameters={
+            "to": ParameterContract("to", Role.AUTHORITY, frozenset({"email"})),
+            "subject": ParameterContract("subject", Role.PAYLOAD),
+            "body": ParameterContract("body", Role.PAYLOAD),
+        },
+        effects=frozenset({Effect.NETWORK_EGRESS, Effect.WRITE}),
+    ),
+    ToolContract(
+        tool="http_get",
+        parameters={"url": ParameterContract("url", Role.AUTHORITY, frozenset({"url"}))},
+        effects=frozenset({Effect.NETWORK_EGRESS, Effect.READ}),
+    ),
+    ToolContract(
+        tool="read_file",
+        parameters={"path": ParameterContract("path", Role.AUTHORITY)},
+        effects=frozenset({Effect.READ}),
+    ),
+]
+
+WORDS = (
+    "incident outage deploy rollback service latency queue cache token report "
+    "summary escalate compliance urgent please note also however therefore"
+).split()
+
+TLDS = ["example", "test", "invalid", "corp.example", "evil.example"]
+
+
+def _word(rng: random.Random) -> str:
+    return rng.choice(WORDS)
+
+
+def _operand(rng: random.Random) -> str:
+    """Generate an authority-shaped value of a random kind."""
+    label = "".join(rng.choices(string.ascii_lowercase, k=rng.randint(2, 8)))
+    host = rng.choice(TLDS)
+    return rng.choice(
+        [
+            f"{label}@{host}",
+            f"https://{host}/{label}",
+            f"/var/{label}/{_word(rng)}.log",
+            f"~/{label}/{_word(rng)}",
+            f"s3://{label}/{_word(rng)}",
+            f"arn:aws:s3:::{label}",
+            f"git@{host}:{label}/repo.git",
+            "".join(rng.choices(string.digits, k=rng.randint(8, 19))),
+            f"0x{''.join(rng.choices('0123456789abcdef', k=40))}",
+        ]
+    )
+
+
+def _prose(rng: random.Random, operands: int = 2) -> str:
+    parts = [_word(rng) for _ in range(rng.randint(3, 12))]
+    for _ in range(operands):
+        parts.insert(rng.randint(0, len(parts)), _operand(rng))
+    text = " ".join(parts)
+    if rng.random() < 0.3:
+        text += rng.choice([".", "!", ")", "]", ",", '"', "\n"])
+    return text
+
+
+def _value(rng: random.Random, depth: int = 0):
+    """An arbitrary argument value, including shapes a tool should never send."""
+    choices = ["str", "int", "float", "bool", "none", "operand"]
+    if depth < 2:
+        choices += ["list", "dict"]
+    kind = rng.choice(choices)
+    if kind == "str":
+        return _prose(rng, operands=rng.randint(0, 1))
+    if kind == "operand":
+        return _operand(rng)
+    if kind == "int":
+        return rng.randint(-10**6, 10**6)
+    if kind == "float":
+        return rng.uniform(-1e4, 1e4)
+    if kind == "bool":
+        return rng.random() < 0.5
+    if kind == "none":
+        return None
+    if kind == "list":
+        return [_value(rng, depth + 1) for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 3))]
+    return {_word(rng): _value(rng, depth + 1) for _ in range(rng.randint(0, 3))}
+
+
+def _session(seed: int, policy: Policy | None = None) -> Session:
+    counter = itertools.count(1)
+    return Session(
+        contracts=ContractRegistry(TOOLS),
+        policy=policy or Policy(denial_budget=-1),
+        sources=[
+            Source("principal", Trust.USER_INPUT),
+            Source("web", Trust.TOOL_UNTRUSTED),
+            Source("directory", Trust.TOOL_TRUSTED, authoritative_for=frozenset({"email"})),
+        ],
+        id_factory=lambda: f"{next(counter):016x}",
+        session_id=f"fuzz-{seed}",
+    )
+
+
+class TestSealingIsComplete:
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize("seed", SEEDS)
+    def test_no_recognised_operand_survives_untrusted_observation(self, seed: int) -> None:
+        rng = random.Random(seed)
+        session = _session(seed)
+        for _ in range(20):
+            text = _prose(rng, operands=rng.randint(0, 3))
+            expected = {m.value for m in extract(text)}
+            sealed = session.observe("web", text)
+            for value in expected:
+                assert value not in sealed, (
+                    f"operand {value!r} survived sealing in {sealed!r}"
+                )
+
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize("seed", SEEDS[:12])
+    def test_sealed_text_contains_one_handle_per_operand(self, seed: int) -> None:
+        rng = random.Random(seed)
+        session = _session(seed)
+        for _ in range(20):
+            text = _prose(rng, operands=rng.randint(0, 3))
+            count = len(extract(text))
+            sealed = session.observe("web", text)
+            assert len(SEAL_PATTERN.findall(sealed)) == count
+
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize("seed", SEEDS[:12])
+    def test_prose_without_operands_is_returned_unchanged(self, seed: int) -> None:
+        """Sealing must be a no-op on text carrying no identifiers -- the
+        property that makes seal-everything safe at the protocol layer."""
+        rng = random.Random(seed)
+        session = _session(seed)
+        for _ in range(20):
+            text = " ".join(_word(rng) for _ in range(rng.randint(3, 20)))
+            if extract(text):
+                continue
+            assert session.observe("web", text) == text
+
+
+class TestMonitorNeverRaises:
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize("seed", SEEDS)
+    def test_arbitrary_arguments_produce_a_verdict(self, seed: int) -> None:
+        """A monitor that crashes on malformed input fails *open* in any
+        harness that catches exceptions and carries on."""
+        rng = random.Random(seed)
+        session = _session(seed)
+        session.observe("principal", _prose(rng, operands=2))
+        for _ in range(30):
+            contract = rng.choice(TOOLS)
+            arguments = {
+                name: _value(rng) for name in contract.parameters if rng.random() < 0.9
+            }
+            if rng.random() < 0.2:
+                arguments[_word(rng)] = _value(rng)  # a parameter no contract declares
+            decision = session.admit(contract.tool, arguments)
+            assert decision.verdict in (Verdict.ALLOW, Verdict.DENY, Verdict.ESCALATE)
+
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize("seed", SEEDS[:12])
+    def test_unknown_tools_and_empty_arguments_are_handled(self, seed: int) -> None:
+        rng = random.Random(seed)
+        session = _session(seed)
+        for _ in range(15):
+            session.admit(_word(rng), {})
+            session.admit(_word(rng), {_word(rng): _value(rng)})
+
+    @pytest.mark.parametrize("seed", SEEDS[:12])
+    def test_hostile_handle_shaped_arguments(self, seed: int) -> None:
